intro: Catalonia has protected individual trees by law since 1987, and cutting one is simply forbidden. There are 299 declared monumental trees in the region and three of them stand within reach of Tarragona on ground anybody can walk onto: a plane filling a village square, a pair of cypresses in a town hall courtyard beside a Cistercian monastery, and a wild pear on a track in the Prades mountains. Readers sent two more holm oaks: one rising out of the scrub above Altafulla, and one arching over an old wall near Tamarit.
meta_description: Tarragona's remarkable trees: a plane that fills a village square, cypresses in a monastery courtyard, a wild pear in the hills and two readers' holm oaks.
question_answer: Nobody publishes ages for Catalonia's monumental trees, so Tarragona's oldest cannot be named. The register records species, condition, height, trunk girth and crown width, and the tallest of the register's three here is the plane of the Riera de Gaià square, 23 metres high.
question_meta: Catalonia's register does not record tree ages, so Tarragona's oldest is unknown. What the register does measure, and 5 trees worth the trip.
question_context: The Catalan register is precise about everything except age. For each declared tree it publishes the species, the condition, the total height, the trunk perimeter at 1.3 metres and the average crown diameter, along with a location to five decimal places and an official record page, and it carries no age column at all. That is a deliberate choice rather than an oversight: dating a living tree without coring it is guesswork, and the register was built to protect trees rather than to date them. What it does record is that these three are alive and in normal condition, which matters more than it sounds, because the same register marks a good number of trees in this province as dead while keeping them listed. So the honest answer for Tarragona is a size rather than an age: the plane of the Riera de Gaià square is 23 metres tall, the register's own figure. Getting there: each stop is a short drive from Tarragona.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Tarragona?
faq.a: Unknown, and the register that protects these trees does not try to answer it. Catalonia records species, condition, height, trunk girth and crown width for each monumental tree and has no age column. The tallest here is the plane of the Riera de Gaià square.

faq.q: What does monumental tree mean in Catalonia?
faq.a: A legal status. Since 1987 individual trees can be declared arbre monumental, after which felling or uprooting them, wholly or partly, is prohibited. There are 299 declared, and 24 more were added in 2025 after nearly a decade with none.

faq.q: Are these trees free to visit?
faq.a: Yes, all five can be seen for free. One stands in a village square, two cypresses in the courtyard of a town hall beside the Santes Creus monastery, one on a track in the Prades mountains, a reader's holm oak above Altafulla is seen from the edge of the scrub, and another reader's oak near Tamarit from the path beside its wall.

Because most of the monumental trees near Tarragona stand on private farms, the mas and the masia, and this site does not send people onto private land. Several fine ones are excluded for that reason, including a holm oak at Mas de Borbo with a trunk 6.45 metres round.

No. They are five separate stops spread over 30 kilometres, between 9 and 29 kilometres from Tarragona; the two oaks near Altafulla and Tamarit are a short train ride up the coast, the others a short drive.

trees.name: The Plane of the Riera de Gaia Square

location.address: Placa de la Vila, La Riera de Gaia 43762, Tarragona

trees.story: This tree is the square. La Riera de Gaia is a small town inland from the coast north of Tarragona, and the plane standing in its Placa de la Vila takes up most of it, which is the way these things went in Catalan villages. A plane was put in the square because it grows fast, casts dense shade by June and can be pollarded hard every few years without complaint, and then it outlived the reason and became the thing the square is named for. Catalonia declared it a monumental tree in 1992, which makes cutting it illegal. It is one of the trees selected for the book Arboles singulares de Espana, where it takes a two-page spread. The register lists it as being in normal condition and puts it at 23 metres tall, but gives no trunk girth at breast height, so this page cannot tell you how thick it is, only that Catalonia thought it worth protecting and that a national survey of Spain's singular trees agreed. If you have measured it, tell us.
trees.access: Free, in the public square in the middle of the village
trees.transport: About 11 km northeast of Tarragona, roughly 15 minutes by car
trees.notes: Declared a Catalan monumental tree in 1992, code MA-36.126.01, condition recorded as normal. The register fitxa gives height 23 m and a 4.97 m trunk figure whose measuring height it does not state, so no girth is recorded (2026-10-13). Also carried in Arboles singulares de Espana (Mundi-Prensa, 2nd ed. 2004, pp. 242 to 243). No age published anywhere.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the tree that fills most of the village square, a pollarded plane declared a monument in 1992. It stands in the Placa de la Vila, La Riera de Gaia.

trees.name: The Cypresses of the Abbot's Palace at Santes Creus

location.address: Pati de l'Ajuntament, Santes Creus, Aiguamurcia 43815, Tarragona

trees.story: Two cypresses in a courtyard at a Cistercian monastery, and the courtyard now belongs to the town hall. Santes Creus was founded in the twelfth century and is one of the three great Cistercian houses of Catalonia, with the kings of Aragon buried in its church; the abbot's palace beside it passed into secular hands after the monasteries were dissolved in 1835, and the local council occupies part of it. The two cypresses stand in its patio, 18 metres tall on trunks 3.37 metres round with crowns only 9.1 metres across, which is the shape of the species: Cupressus sempervirens grows as a dark green column and almost nothing else, which is why it has been planted at monasteries and cemeteries around the Mediterranean for two thousand years. Catalonia has them on its monumental tree register as a pair. The status listed is that the declaration is pending rather than complete, so they are on the list and protection is still working its way through. Nobody has published an age.
trees.access: Free, in the town hall courtyard at Santes Creus, beside the monastery
trees.transport: About 27 km north of Tarragona, roughly 35 minutes by car
trees.notes: One entry for the pair, as the register lists them. Code MA-01.001.01. Height 18 m, trunk perimeter 3.37 m and crown 9.1 m are the register's, given for the first tree catalogued. Status is recorded as AM previst, declaration foreseen rather than completed, which the story states. No age published.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as a matched pair of dark, column-shaped cypresses, 3.37 metres round. They stand in the town hall courtyard beside the monastery at Santes Creus.

trees.name: The Wild Pear of El Cisterer
trees.age_estimate: roughly 75 to 150 years, judged from a trunk 1.97 m round
trees.story: Catalonia protects 299 trees and one of them is a wild pear, which tells you something about how the list was made. Pyrus spinosa is a thorny scrubby thing of dry Mediterranean hillsides, usually a bush and rarely worth a second look, and this one is 10.5 metres tall with a trunk just under two metres round and a crown 16 metres across, which for the species is enormous. It stands at Cap del Plans above Prades, on the right of the track, in the Prades mountains where the ground is red sandstone and the villages sit above 900 metres. It was declared a monumental tree in 1991. The register puts its condition as normal. What makes it worth the drive is not size in absolute terms, since almost every other tree on this site is bigger, but the fact that this is the species performing at the top of its range: a hedgerow shrub that got left alone long enough to become a tree. The register itself gives no age, as with every Catalan entry; the 75 to 150 years shown here is judged from the girth.
trees.access: Free, on the right of a public track above the village
trees.transport: About 29 km northwest of Tarragona in the Prades mountains, roughly 40 minutes by car
trees.notes: Declared a Catalan monumental tree in 1991, condition normal. Height 10.5 m, trunk perimeter 1.97 m, crown 16.0 m from the register. No age published. The coordinate is the register's own; the location description places it beside a track at Cap del Plans, which is why precision is marked approximate rather than confirmed.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as a wild pear grown to tree size, 10.5 metres tall with a crown 16 across, where the species is usually a hillside bush. It stands on the right of the track above the village.
trees.verify_notes: Age derived from girth, not from a source: 197 cm at Mitchell's 2.5 to 1.5 cm of girth a year for an open-grown to shaded temperate broadleaf. Any measured or documented age replaces this outright.

trees.name: The Holm Oak above the Scrub at Altafulla

location.address: Scrubland by Carrer dels Avellaners, upper Altafulla, Tarragonès
location.neighbourhood: Altafulla (a short train ride up the coast from Tarragona)

trees.how_to_recognise: The one big tree rising out of the scrub: a broad dark dome of evergreen oak, far taller and wider than the young pines and broom in front of it, its grey trunk forking low down.
trees.access: The reader photographed it from the edge of the scrub near Carrer dels Avellaners, in the upper part of Altafulla. We have not confirmed who owns the ground it stands on, so look from where they stood.
trees.story:
A reader on the hillside above Altafulla, a few kilometres up the coast from Tarragona, sent us this oak, photographed from where they stood looking at it.

It is easy to see why they stopped. Everything around it is young: pines no taller than a person, yellow broom, the dense low green of Mediterranean scrub. Out of the middle of it rises one great evergreen oak, its crown a broad dark dome many times the size of anything near it, its grey trunk forking low into heavy limbs. To our eyes it is a holm oak, the alzina of Catalonia, whose small, tough, dark leaves give the crown that close, almost woolly look; tell us if you know it better.

We do not know its age or girth, how long the ground around it has been scrub, or who has looked after it. If you do, tell us here and we will add it as yours, and if you can stand closer, a photograph of the trunk would help the next person find it.

Come towards evening, when the crown stands dark against a pale sky and the scrub below it turns gold.

trees.name: The Oak over the Wall at Tamarit

location.address: Beside Carrer del Marqués de Tamarit, near the Mineta del Sifó spring, Tamarit, Tarragona 43893
location.neighbourhood: Tamarit (on the coast between Tarragona and Altafulla)

trees.how_to_recognise: Above an old wall of stone and brick with a brick pillar in it: a big evergreen oak whose one great dark limb arches out over the path like a doorway, the crown of small dull leaves above.
trees.access: The reader photographed it from the path beside the wall. We have not confirmed who owns the ground behind the wall, so look from the path.
trees.story:
A reader on the coast between Tarragona and Altafulla, near Tamarit, stopped under this oak and sent us the photograph they took looking straight up into it.

The tree grows above an old wall. The wall runs down the left of the picture, rough stone at the foot and brick higher up, with a brick pillar rising out of the greenery, and the oak stands on the ground behind and above it. One great dark limb leaves the trunk and arcs right out over the path, low enough to frame a window of blue sky, before it turns back up into the crown. Above that the tree divides again and again into grey, twisting branches under a canopy of small, dull leaves lit gold by a low sun.

To our eyes it is a holm oak, the alzina that grows wild along this coast and can live for centuries when it is left alone; tell us if you know it better. We do not know its age or girth, who built the wall, or whose ground it stands on. If you do, tell us here and we will add it as yours.

Come late in the afternoon, as the reader did, and walk under the arching limb.
